Fix an integer $N\ge1$, put $h=1/N$, and let $x_j=jh$ for $j=0,\ldots,N$. The cells are $K_j=[x_{j-1},x_j]$. For $g_0,g_1\in\mathbb R$, let $S_h(g_0,g_1)$ be the finite-dimensional space of continuous functions on $[0,1]$ that are affine on each cell and have endpoint values $g_0,g_1$. Write $V_h=S_h(0,0)$ for the homogeneous test and trial space. “P1” means polynomial degree at most one on each interval.

Let $\epsilon>0$, $b\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, and $f\in C([0,1])$. The stationary boundary-value problem is to find $u\in C^2([0,1])$ such that $-\epsilon u''+b u'=f$ on $(0,1)$, with prescribed endpoint values $u(0)=g_0$ and $u(1)=g_1$. Its dimensionless cell Péclet number is $\mathrm{Pe}=|b|h/(2\epsilon)>0$. The stability theorem on this page uses the homogeneous branch $g_0=g_1=0$; the general endpoint notation also permits the boundary-layer example.

derivations.claim: Fix a cell $K=[a,b]$ of length $h_K$, and let $s_K=(u(b)-u(a))/h_K$ be the slope of $I_hu$ on $K$. By the fundamental theorem of calculus, $s_K=h_K^{-1}\int_a^b u'(t)\,dt$. For every $x\in K$, the same theorem gives $|u'(x)-u'(t)|\le h_K\|u''\|_\infty$, so averaging in $t$ yields $|(u-I_hu)'(x)|=|u'(x)-s_K|\le h_K\|u''\|_\infty$.

Since $(u-I_hu)(a)=0$, integrating the derivative bound from step 1.1 over $[a,x]$ gives $|u(x)-I_hu(x)|\le h_K^2\|u''\|_\infty$ for every $x\in K$. Therefore $\|u-I_hu\|_{L^2(K)}^2\le h_K^5\|u''\|_\infty^2$.

The cell interiors are disjoint, their lengths sum to $1$, and $h_K\le h$, so $\sum_Kh_K^5\le h^4\sum_Kh_K=h^4$. Summing step 2.1 over the cells and taking nonnegative square roots proves the estimate.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

Fix $d\ge2$ and a bounded connected polyhedral open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$. For each mesh parameter $h$, let $\mathcal T_h$ be a finite matching shape-regular affine simplicial mesh in the sense of [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]], and put $h=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}h_K$. Let $V_h$ be the space of continuous functions on $\overline\Omega$ that are affine on every cell and vanish on $\partial\Omega$.

Let $\epsilon>0$, $b\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$, $c\in C(\overline\Omega)$, and $f\in C(\overline\Omega)$. Define $B:=\|b\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}$ and $C:=\|c\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}$. Assume a fixed $\omega>0$ satisfies $c-\frac12\nabla\cdot b\ge\omega$ on $\Omega$. The boundary condition for this branch is $u=0$ on the whole boundary, including the inflow part $\{x\in\partial\Omega:b(x)\cdot n(x)<0\}$. A classical exact solution is a function $u\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$ satisfying $-\epsilon\Delta u+b\cdot\nabla u+cu=f$ in $\Omega$ and this boundary condition.

derivations.claim: Fix a cell $K$ and a vertex $a_0$. Taylor's formula along the segment from $a_0$ to $x\in K$ gives $u(x)=p_K(x)+r_K(x)$ with $p_K(x)=u(a_0)+\nabla u(a_0)\cdot(x-a_0)$, $|r_K(x)|\le\frac12h_K^2\|D^2u\|_{L^\infty(K)}$, and $|\nabla r_K(x)|\le h_K\|D^2u\|_{L^\infty(K)}$.

The nodal interpolant reproduces $p_K$, so $u-I_Ku=r_K-\sum_i r_K(a_i)\lambda_i$. On $K$, $0\le\lambda_i\le1$ and $\sum_i\lambda_i=1$. The altitude from any vertex to its opposite facet is at least $\rho_K$, hence $|\nabla\lambda_i|\le\rho_K^{-1}\le\sigma h_K^{-1}$ by [F1]. Substitution of the bounds in step 1.1 gives $|u-I_Ku|\le C(d)h_K^2\|D^2u\|_{L^\infty(K)}$ and $|\nabla(u-I_Ku)|\le C(d,\sigma)h_K\|D^2u\|_{L^\infty(K)}$.

Squaring the two pointwise bounds, integrating on each cell, summing over the finite mesh, using $h_K\le h$ and $\sum_K|K|=|\Omega|$, and taking square roots proves both global estimates with $M_2=|\Omega|^{1/2}\|D^2u\|_\infty$.

On a shared interior facet, the affine traces from its two incident cells agree at all facet vertices, so they agree everywhere on that facet; thus the cell interpolants assemble to a continuous $I_hu$. If $u$ vanishes on a boundary facet, all its vertices there have zero nodal values, so the affine trace also vanishes there. This proves both global conformity and the boundary claim.

Let $X_c$ and $X_f$ be finite-dimensional real vector spaces and set $X=X_c\oplus X_f$; elements are written $(u_c,u_f)$, with $u_c$ the resolved component and $u_f$ the unresolved component. For a real vector space $Y$, let $Y^*$ be its space of real linear functionals. Let $A_{cc}:X_c\to X_c^*$, $A_{cf}:X_f\to X_c^*$, $A_{fc}:X_c\to X_f^*$, and $A_{ff}:X_f\to X_f^*$ be linear maps, with $A_{ff}$ invertible, and let $F_c\in X_c^*$ and $F_f\in X_f^*$. The linear equation on $X$ has block form
$$\begin{pmatrix}A_{cc}&A_{cf}\\A_{fc}&A_{ff}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}u_c\\u_f\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}F_c\\F_f\end{pmatrix}.$$
The fine residual for a resolved vector $v_c$ is $r_f(v_c):=F_f-A_{fc}v_c$. Exact elimination gives $u_f=A_{ff}^{-1}r_f(u_c)$ and the Schur equation
$$\left(A_{cc}-A_{cf}A_{ff}^{-1}A_{fc}\right)u_c=F_c-A_{cf}A_{ff}^{-1}F_f.$$

A **residual closure** selects a linear map $T:X_f^*\to X_f$ to approximate the exact inverse $A_{ff}^{-1}:X_f^*\to X_f$. It defines $\widetilde A_{cc}:=A_{cc}-A_{cf}TA_{fc}$, $\widetilde F_c:=F_c-A_{cf}TF_f$, and the modeled fine component $\widetilde u_f:=T r_f(\widetilde u_c)$, where $\widetilde u_c$ solves $\widetilde A_{cc}\widetilde u_c=\widetilde F_c$. This is a finite-dimensional algebraic closure; an application to a PDE requires its own residual, spaces, invertibility, and approximation-defect analysis.

derivations.claim: Write the exact Schur operator and load as $S=A_{cc}-A_{cf}GA_{fc}$ and $g=F_c-A_{cf}GF_f$, so $Su_c=g$. Put $\Delta:=T-G$. The approximate quantities satisfy $\widetilde S=S-A_{cf}\Delta A_{fc}$ and $\widetilde g=g-A_{cf}\Delta F_f$.

Since $\widetilde S\widetilde u_c=\widetilde g$, step 1.1 gives $\widetilde S(\widetilde u_c-u_c)=\widetilde g-\widetilde S u_c=-A_{cf}\Delta(F_f-A_{fc}u_c)=-A_{cf}\Delta r_f$. Apply the induced operator norms and multiply by $\|\widetilde S^{-1}\|$ to prove the coarse bound.

The exact fine component is $u_f=G r_f$. The modeled component is $\widetilde u_f=T(r_f-A_{fc}(\widetilde u_c-u_c))$. Subtracting gives $\widetilde u_f-u_f=(T-G)r_f-TA_{fc}(\widetilde u_c-u_c)$. The triangle inequality and operator norms give the stated fine-scale bound.
